blocks.text: By the 1960s the government wanted banking to serve social goals: welfare, credit for needy sectors such as **agriculture and small and village industries**, a check on private monopolies and a smaller gap between regions. The privately owned commercial banks were not helping to reach these goals, so the government took them over. The first step came on **19 July 1969**, when **14 major commercial banks** were nationalised. The test was size: every bank with deposits above **₹50 crore** was taken over.

blocks.title: Objectives of nationalisation
items: Steer bank credit to the **priority sector**: agriculture and allied activities, small-scale industries and small businesses.
Create a **new class of entrepreneurs** to build and speed up economic growth.
Give bank staff proper training and a reasonable term of service.
End the **concentration of economic power** in a few hands.
**Professionalise** bank management.
Build public confidence in the banking system.
Stop bank funds being used for anti-social activities.
Take banking to **unbanked rural areas**.
**Mobilise national savings** and channel them into productive uses.

blocks.title: Odd one out
blocks.text: Nationalisation aimed at credit for agriculture, SMEs and exports, not at lending to **big industries only**. If an option says credit for big industry alone, it is the wrong one.

blocks.title: Why nationalise: P-A-R-S-E-C
blocks.phrase: A PARSEC is a huge distance, and banking had to travel just as far: Priority, Anti-social use stopped, Rural, Savings, Entrepreneurs, Concentration ended.
letters: Priority sector credit (agriculture, small industry, small business)
blocks.note: Professional management, staff training and public confidence were also objectives.

blocks.title: Remember the 14 banks of 1969
blocks.phrase: Cats Make Delicious Pies; Sheep Chew Indian Ice; Bears Undoubtedly Adore United UCO Bananas.
blocks.note: Federal, HDFC, ICICI and other private banks were not in this list.

blocks.text: The process was repeated in **1980**, when another **six banks** were nationalised under the **Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1980**. The stated reason was to give the government more control over **credit delivery**. After this second phase the government controlled about **91 per cent** of the banking business in India. The date usually quoted is **15 April 1980**.

sections.title: SBI, its associates and the 2017 merger

blocks.text: Until the **Reserve Bank of India** was set up in 1935, the **Imperial Bank of India** (now SBI) also carried out some central banking functions along with commercial banking. Today SBI acts as the **agent of RBI** at places where RBI has no branch of its own.

blocks.title: How SBI absorbed its associate banks
items: The **State Bank of India (Subsidiary Banks) Act** is passed. Under it, **8 subsidiaries** of SBI come into being.
SBI merges State Bank of **Jaipur** (founded 1943) and State Bank of **Bikaner** (founded 1944) to form **State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur**.
**State Bank of Saurashtra** merges with SBI.
**State Bank of Indore** (founded 1920) merges with SBI, leaving **5** associate banks.
The remaining **five associate banks** and **Bharatiya Mahila Bank** merge with SBI.

blocks.text: Once the subsidiaries ceased to exist, the government repealed the **SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959** and the **State Bank of Hyderabad Act, 1956**, and removed provisions about subsidiaries from the **SBI Act, 1955**. The aim of the merger was to pool resources, cut costs, lower the cost of funds and improve productivity and customer service. SBI negotiated with the five banks with the Centre’s sanction and in consultation with RBI, and the schemes took effect from **1 April 2017**.

blocks.title: Positive impact
items: After the two phases, roughly **80 per cent** of the banking sector came under public sector ownership.
Big push to **branch expansion** in unbanked, rural and semi-urban areas.
Huge **deposit mobilisation**, which raised the economy’s savings rate.
More **lending to agriculture** and allied sectors.
As quoted in the syllabus, deposits grew by about **800 per cent** and advances by about **11,000 per cent**.
Government ownership gave the public **implicit faith** in the safety of public sector banks.

blocks.title: Limitations of nationalisation
rows: Large parts of the country, especially backward states such as Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and the north-eastern states, stayed unbanked.
Funds raised were not enough for the economy’s needs, and allocation did not always match requirements.
Political pressure and unprofessional working reduced efficiency and profitability.
Huge branch expansion, large staff, administrative costs and union struggles pushed expenses to dangerous levels.
Seen in loan melas; it led to heavy non-performing assets (NPAs) and inefficiency.

blocks.text: Other weaknesses included poor infrastructure and weak competitiveness. Lethargic working, lack of accountability and no profit motive turned many banks into loss-making units. After the **economic reforms of 1991** the industry entered a new phase of competition, efficiency and productivity.

blocks.title: 80% or 91%?
blocks.text: Two figures appear in study material: about **91 per cent of banking business** under government control after 1980, and about **80 per cent of the banking sector** in public ownership. Both come from the 2024-25 syllabus; for a question that quotes one, pick the matching option.

sections.title: Steps before reforms: IDBI, RBI and BR Act

blocks.text: Commercial banks traditionally met the **short-term** needs of industry, trade and agriculture. Long-term finance was left to other agencies or the government, and the two sides did not coordinate. To supply long-term funds for industrial projects, the government set up the **Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI)** in **1964**.

blocks.title: Milestones in regulating banks
items: **Reserve Bank of India** established in April.
**Industrial Policy Resolution** adopted; it envisaged a **mixed economy** and more state involvement in banking and finance.
RBI nationalised under the **Reserve Bank of India (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948**.
**Banking Regulation Act** gives RBI power to regulate, control and inspect banks.
**IDBI** set up for long-term industrial finance.
First nationalisation of 14 banks.
Second nationalisation of 6 banks.

blocks.title: What the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 provided
items: RBI may **regulate, control and inspect** banks in India.
No new bank, and no new branch of an existing bank, without an **RBI licence**.
No two banks may have **common directors**.

blocks.title: RBI timeline
blocks.text: RBI was **set up in 1935** but **nationalised on 1 January 1949**. The Banking Regulation Act (1949) came the same year.

sections.title: The 1990s reforms and new private banks

blocks.text: A key feature of the 1990s reforms was permission to open **new private sector banks**. The aim of reforms since 1991 is a vibrant, efficient, competitive financial sector that responds to the needs of the economy. The focus was on strengthening financial institutions and linking the domestic financial system with the global banking and economic system.

blocks.title: What reform policies aimed to give banks
items: Greater **flexibility** in banking operations.
Greater **accountability to shareholders**.
Greater **control** over bank functions.
**Safety** through prudential norms and supervision.

blocks.title: Reform aims: F-A-C-S
blocks.phrase: Reforms made banks FACS-ready: Flexibility, Accountability, Control, Safety.

blocks.text: On **14 August 1991** the government set up a high-level **Committee on the Financial System (CFS)** to look at the structure, organisation, functions and procedures of the financial system. Based on its recommendations, a comprehensive reform of the banking system began in **1992-93**. In **December 1997** another committee on banking sector reforms was set up under **M. Narasimham**. It reviewed progress and charted a programme to make India’s financial system stronger and internationally competitive. This **Narasimham Committee-II** submitted its report in **April 1998**.

blocks.title: Main suggestions of Narasimham Committee-II
items: Stronger banks: **merge** strong PSBs and development financial institutions (DFIs); **close** weak, unviable ones.
A **3-tier banking structure** after mergers (see the pyramid below).
Higher **CRAR** (capital to risk-weighted assets ratio), raised to **10 per cent**.
**Budgetary recapitalisation** of PSBs is not viable and should be dropped.
Strengthen the legal framework for **loan recovery**; the government later passed the **SARFAESI Act, 2002**.
Cut **net NPAs** to about **3 per cent by 2002** (with an interim target for 2000).
**Rationalise** branches and staff of PSBs.
Continue **licensing new private banks**, domestic as well as foreign.
**Depoliticise** bank boards under RBI supervision.

blocks.title: Suggested 3-tier banking structure
items: Tier 1: 2-3 banks
International orientation
Tier 2: 8-10 banks
National orientation
Tier 3: many banks
Local banks

blocks.title: Pyramid of banks: 3-10-Many
blocks.phrase: Top: a few global giants; middle: ten national; base: loads of local banks. Think “2-3, 8-10, Many”.
letters: A large number of local banks
blocks.note: CFS was set up in August 1991; Narasimham Committee-II in December 1997 with its report in April 1998.

blocks.title: Dates to hold on to
blocks.text: CFS formed **14 Aug 1991**; reforms began **1992-93**; Narasimham Committee-II formed **Dec 1997**, report **Apr 1998**; SARFAESI Act **2002**.

blocks.title: Why merge?
blocks.text: Fewer, larger banks are stronger, cut costs and are better placed to lend. This follows the thinking of the Narasimham committees, which also suggested mergers of strong banks.
